q: Before excavation begins on a construction site, what should the Architect and project team verify to minimize the risk of construction errors, property disputes, and accidental damage to existing services?
o: Approved construction benchmarks, reference points, and layout control markers
Soil conditions, equipment access routes, and temporary drainage provisions
Site conditions, property boundaries, and utility locations
Existing easements, right-of-way limits, and adjacent property improvements
n: Before excavation, the team checks site conditions, property boundaries and underground utilities. This avoids layout errors, boundary disputes and damage to existing services. Source: NBC (PD 1096) IRR, Rule XI (protection of adjoining property and utilities); DOLE OSHS Construction Safety (excavation).

q: A developer engages an architect to prepare a subdivision development plan for a 12-hectare property. Before any survey verification, site planning, or subdivision layout can proceed, the architect must first determine whether the client has legal rights over the land. Which document provides the strongest evidence of such ownership?
n: The Transfer Certificate of Title, under the Torrens system, is the strongest proof of ownership. Tax declarations, the CAR and tax clearances are only supporting documents. Source: PD 1529 (Property Registration Decree), Secs. 39–43.

q: Who issues lot titles in the Philippines?
n: Certificates of title are entered and issued by the Register of Deeds of the province or city where the land lies. The Register of Deeds operates under the LRA. Source: PD 1529 (Property Registration Decree), Secs. 10, 39–40.

q: Before a subdivision development application can proceed, the developer must secure a document confirming that the proposed project conforms with the municipality's Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP), zoning ordinance, and allowable land use regulations. What document serves this purpose?
n: A Locational Clearance confirms that the project conforms to the CLUP and zoning ordinance. It is required before the development permit and building permit. Source: PD 957 Revised IRR; HLURB/DHSUD Locational Clearance rules.

q: Prior to committing a property for subdivision development, a developer conducts a comprehensive evaluation covering topography, access, drainage, utilities, environmental conditions, hazard susceptibility, and development constraints in order to determine the site's overall suitability for the intended project. What is this process called?
n: Site suitability analysis evaluates topography, access, drainage, utilities, environment, hazards and constraints to judge a site's overall fitness for a project. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 201 (site analysis); HLURB CLUP Guidebook (land suitability).

q: During subdivision planning, which phase focuses on determining the overall layout, capacity, and interrelationship of roads, drainage facilities, water distribution systems, sewerage networks, electrical systems, and other essential services needed to support the proposed development?
n: Infrastructure planning sets the layout, capacity and relationships of roads, drainage, water, sewer, power and other services that support the development. Source: PD 957 / BP 220 Revised IRR (design standards for site development and utilities).

q: During the early stages of subdivision development, which phase focuses on establishing the overall vision and preliminary framework of the project, including the arrangement of roads, open spaces, residential blocks, community facilities, land-use relationships, and future development direction before detailed planning and engineering design are undertaken?
n: Conceptual master planning sets the overall vision and preliminary framework (roads, open spaces, blocks, facilities, land-use relationships) before detailed planning and engineering. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 203 (Physical Planning).

q: A document issued to a land owner when such land is registered for the very first time under the Torrens system of land registration
n: An Original Certificate of Title is issued when land is registered under the Torrens system for the first time. Later transfers produce TCTs. Source: PD 1529 (Property Registration Decree), Sec. 39.

q: Which government agency is primarily responsible for overseeing economic and regional planning, including providing guidance to Local Government Units (LGUs) to ensure that LGUs align their development plans with national and regional goals?
n: NEDA (now the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development under RA 12145) oversees economic and regional planning. Through the Regional Development Councils, it guides LGUs in aligning their plans with national and regional goals. Source: EO 230 (1987); RA 12145 (2025).

q: Which national agency was created under Republic Act No. 11201 enacted in 2019, replacing the Housing and Land Use Regulatory Board (HLURB) and consolidating housing policy, urban development, and land use regulation functions in the Philippines?
o: Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development
Local Government Housing and Urban Planning Council
n: RA 11201 (2019) created the DHSUD. It took over the policy and regulatory functions of the HLURB and HUDCC. Source: RA 11201 (Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development Act), Secs. 4–5.

q: It plays a crucial role in dictating building height restrictions, especially in areas close to airports.
o: Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP)
n: The CAAP sets obstacle limitation surfaces and height clearances for structures near airports. Source: RA 9497 (Civil Aviation Authority Act of 2008); CAAP height clearance permit rules.

q: As per the Philippine Green Building Code, an escalator/moving ramp/walkway shall automatically be put on standby mode when no activity has been detected for a maximum of
n: Escalators, moving ramps and walkways must go to standby automatically when no activity is detected for a maximum of five minutes. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), Sec. 10.6.5.

q: As per the Philippine Green Building Code, lighting shall switch off after the elevator has been inactive for a maximum of
n: Elevator car lighting must switch off after the elevator has been inactive for a maximum of five minutes. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), Sec. 10.6.5.

q: As per the Philippine Green Building Code, in order to reduce energy consumption, overhead or elevated water storage shall be integrated in the water distribution system. However, buildings below how many storeys are exempted?
n: Overhead or elevated water storage must be part of the water distribution system to save pumping energy. Buildings below ten storeys are exempt. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), Sec. 10.6.7.

q: Which of the following is traditionally regarded as the primary basis for Direct Selection of an Architect for a relatively small project?
o: The Architect's availability during the project timeline
The Client's preference for a specific design style
Proximity of the Architect's office to the project site
n: Direct selection suits relatively small projects. The client picks the architect by reputation, acquaintance or recommendation. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Annex A, Sec. C (Selection of the Architect).

q: According to the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), what is the first step in the Comparative Selection of an Architect?
n: Comparative selection proceeds as Invitation (with the ToR), Pre-qualification, Interview, Verification, Evaluation and Ranking, and Negotiation. Invitation comes first. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Annex A, Sec. C.3.2.1.

q: A homeowner plans a minor residential renovation involving interior reconfiguration, repainting, and small structural adjustments. The project is modest in scale and requires quick mobilization. Under the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) and the IRR of R.A. 9266, what is the appropriate method of selecting the architect for this type of small project?
n: A small, quick-mobilizing residential job calls for direct selection, based on reputation or recommendation. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Annex A, Sec. C (Direct Selection).

q: During the Contract Document Phase, what is the Architect's primary responsibility in coordinating the project before construction begins?
o: Assist the owner in selecting the most qualified contractor through bid evaluation and negotiation
Review and coordinate all construction documents prepared by the architect, engineers, and other consultants to ensure consistency and completeness
Assist the owner in securing the necessary government approvals and building permit requirements
Update the probable project construction cost and bidding information based on the completed contract documents
n: In the Contract Document phase the architect coordinates and checks the drawings and specifications of the architect, engineers and consultants for consistency and completeness. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Contract Document Phase.

q: A small architectural firm has been commissioned to design a residential project but does not maintain an in-house engineering team. What is the architect's primary responsibility in ensuring the completeness of the construction documents?
o: Require the owner to directly manage all communication among consultants to avoid conflicts in the design documents.
Coordinate with allied professionals while maintaining overall design responsibility and ensuring that all contract documents are properly integrated and consistent.
Limit responsibility to the architectural documents since each consultant is independently liable for his or her own discipline.
Delegate the coordination of all technical documents to the engineering consultants once they have signed and sealed their respective plans.
n: Even when engineers sign their own plans, the architect as prime professional coordinates them and keeps overall responsibility for an integrated, consistent set of contract documents. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202 (architect as prime professional; coordination of engineering work).

q: A government cultural agency plans to develop a new National Performing Arts Center intended to serve as a landmark civic facility. Because the project requires a wide range of conceptual design approaches, the agency wants to obtain creative solutions from multiple architects and have the proposals judged on the basis of comparative excellence. According to the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP) and the IRR of R.A. 9266, which method of selecting an architect is appropriate for this type of large. publicly significant project?
n: A landmark public project that needs creative solutions judged on comparative excellence suits an architectural design competition. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 208 (Architectural Design Competition); SPP Annex A, Sec. C.

q: A private university plans to expand its campus and is looking for an architect who can handle a multi-building academic development. The institution wants to review the qualifications. experience, track record. and methodology of several architects before choosing one. They will prepare a short list, request technical proposals, and evaluate each architect based on credentials and capability rather than conceptual design submission. According to the Standards of Professional Practice (SPP), which method of selecting an architect is appropriate for this type of project?
n: Shortlisting architects and comparing their credentials, experience and methodology, without design submissions, is comparative selection. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Annex A, Sec. C.3.2.

q: What is the coverage of SPP Document 205?
n: SPP Document 205 covers Post-Construction Services. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, list of SPP Documents 201–209.

q: What is SPP 207 about?
n: SPP Document 207 covers Design-Build Services. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, list of SPP Documents 201–209.

q: When the architect prepares the complete construction drawings, technical specifications, updates the SPPCC and assist the owner in filing the required documents to secure the building permit
n: In the Contract Document phase the architect prepares the construction drawings and specifications, updates the SPPCC, and helps the owner file for the building permit. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Contract Document Phase.

q: When the architect makes decisions on all claims of the owner and contractor/s on all matters relating to the execution and progress of work or the interpretation of the contract documents
n: During construction the architect decides on claims of the owner and contractor about the execution and progress of the work and the interpretation of the contract documents. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Construction Phase.

q: A newly completed hotel has turned over its operations to the Architect under a post-construction services agreement. As part of the Architect's responsibilities, they are tasked to innovate schemes to attain maximum building occupancy, particularly for long-term and corporate clients, and to bill tenants and concessionaire for rentals and utilities such as electricity, water, telephone, cable, gas, and other related dues. Under SPP Document 205, these responsibilities fall under
n: Devising schemes to maximize occupancy and billing tenants and concessionaires for rent and utilities fall under Business Development and Supervision Management. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205 (Post-Construction Services, scope).

q: A newly completed mid-rise residential building has turned over its outdoor areas to the architect for post-construction administration. Part of the architect's responsibilities includes supervising landscape contractors and gardeners for proper watering, pruning, trimming, and maintenance of both hardscape and softscape, as well as maintaining orderly entrances, exits, and parking areas, and ensuring that streets, RROWs, walkways, and ramps are properly maintained. Under SPP Document 205, these duties fall under
n: Supervising landscape contractors and gardeners, keeping entrances, exits and parking orderly, and maintaining walkways and ramps fall under Grounds and Landscaping. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205.

q: In a newly completed mixed-use building, the architect is engaged to oversee post-construction operations. Part of the architect's duties includes seeing to it that the building and all its parts (structure, plumbing, electrical, partitions, finishes, etc.) are in good condition, formulating and enforcing rules for the proper use of common areas and emergency/fire exit areas, monitoring security services, and monitoring maintenance and upkeep services such as cleanliness of corridors, lobbies, stairs, exits, parking areas, and garbage collection. Under SPP Document 205, these responsibilities fall under
n: Keeping the building and its parts in good condition, enforcing rules for common and emergency areas, and monitoring security and upkeep fall under Building Maintenance. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205.

q: A commercial building has just completed turnover, and the Architect is now engaged for post-construction services. Part of the Architect's responsibilities includes assisting the proper third parties in seeing to it that all equipment—such as air-conditioning systems, sprinkler systems, generators, transformers, and telecommunications equipment—-are properly maintained and in good working condition, Under SPP Document 205, this responsibility falls under
n: Seeing that equipment such as air-conditioning, sprinklers, generators, transformers and telecom systems is properly maintained falls under Building Equipment Maintenance. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 205.

q: It is the second phase under the scope of services of Regular Design Services.
n: The phases of Regular Design Services are Project Definition, Schematic Design, Design Development, Contract Documents, Bidding/Negotiation and Construction. The second is Schematic Design. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 2.

q: It is the fourth phase under the scope of services of Regular Design Services
n: The fourth phase of Regular Design Services is the Contract Document Phase. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Sec. 2.

q: Under SPP Document 202 on Regular Design Services, during which phase shall the Architect prepare change orders and gather written guarantees required of the Contractor and Sub-Contractors for turnover to the Owner?
n: During the Construction Phase the architect prepares change orders and gathers the written guarantees required of the contractor and subcontractors for turnover to the owner. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202, Construction Phase.

q: Printed documents stipulating procedural and administrative aspects of the contract.
n: The General Conditions are the printed document setting out the procedural and administrative parts of the contract. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Definitions.

q: A duly notarized written contract or equivalent public instrument stipulating the scope of services and guaranteeing compensation of such services to be rendered by an architect registered and licensed under RA 9266.
n: A Service Agreement is a notarized written contract or equivalent public instrument stating the scope of services and guaranteeing the architect's compensation. Source: RA 9266, Sec. 3 (definition of Service Agreement).

q: Which component of the Contract Documents is formally recognized as the graphical presentation of the work, defining the scope, extent, and physical characteristics of the project?
n: The drawings are the graphical presentation of the work. They define its scope, extent and physical character. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Contract Documents.

q: A client repeatedly requests significant revisions to an architect's design. Over time, the revisions have become extensive, continuous, and clearly beyond the scope contemplated in the original Service Agreement. The architect believes that the additional work is no longer covered by the agreed professional fee. What is the MOST appropriate course of action?
o: Inform the client that the requested revisions constitute additional services and negotiate appropriate compensation and terms before proceeding.
Complete the revisions first and seek reimbursement from the client upon project completion.
Suspend all architectural services immediately until the client agrees to stop requesting revisions.
Continue accommodating all revisions as part of professional courtesy to preserve the client relationship and get future projects and referrals from the client.
n: Revisions beyond the agreed scope are additional services. The architect should tell the client and agree on extra compensation and terms before proceeding. Source: 2016 Architect's Guidelines, SPP Doc. 202 (Additional Services); SPP Doc. 200 (Code of Ethical Conduct).

q: Special Instructions which are issued prior to bidding to supplement and/or modify the Drawings, Specifications and/or General Conditions of the Contract.
n: A Bid Bulletin is additional information or instructions issued to bidders before the bidding date that supplement or modify the drawings, specifications or general conditions. Source: UAP Doc. 301 / CIAP Document 102, Definitions.

q: Written or printed description of work describing qualities of materials and mode of construction.
n: Specifications are the written or printed description of the work: material quality and mode of construction. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Definitions.

q: During construction, the contractor privately meets with the owner and proposes changing the architect-specified waterproofing membrane to a cheaper "equivalent" brand, claiming it will save ₱180,000. The owner verbally agrees and instructs the contractor to proceed immediately. The architect is not informed, and the change is not documented in any written instruction, revision, or change order. Weeks later, the architect discovers the substitution during a site inspection. Under standard contract law, RA 9266, and specification principles, which statement best describes the legal and professional status of the substitution?
o: The substitution is valid because the contractor acted in good faith and the cheaper material met the same ASTM performance standards.
The substitution is invalid because only the architect can approve material changes, and the contractor is liable for unauthorized deviation regardless of the owner's consent.
The substitution is invalid only if the architect can prove that the cheaper material caused actual damage or failure in the completed work.
The substitution is valid because the owner has ultimate authority over materials and can override the architect's specifications at any time.
n: Any change to specified materials must go through a written change order or instruction issued through the architect. An undocumented verbal substitution is invalid, and the contractor answers for the unauthorized deviation. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Changes in the Work; RA 9266, Sec. 20.

q: During construction of a mixed-use building, the contractor discovered that the approved plumbing layout conflicted with a proposed firewall. Without prior written approval from the architect, the contractor shifted the firewall by 300 mm to accommodate the plumbing system. Several weeks later, the architect discovered the deviation during a site inspection. What is the MOST appropriate action for the architect?
o: Accept the modification provided the Contractor can demonstrate that the plumbing installation functions properly and does not affect occupancy.
Permit the deviation to remain if the Owner agrees that the modification improves constructability.
Ratify the revised location through a field instruction since reconstruction may result in unnecessary delay and additional cost.
Direct the Contractor to restore the work to the approved plans and specifications unless the deviation is formally evaluated and approved through the proper contract modification process.
n: Work that departs from the approved plans without written approval must be restored, unless the change is formally evaluated and approved through a change order. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Changes in the Work; NBC Sec. 212 (unauthorized changes are a grave violation).

q: During construction, the Contractor discovers a conflict between the approved architectural drawings and the actual site conditions. Instead of requesting clarification, the Contractor proceeds to modify the work based on his own judgment and subsequently JA 143 submits the revisions to the Architect for approval. What is the MOST appropriate action for the Architect?
o: Accept the revisions provided that the Owner agrees with the changes and additional costs.
Approve the revisions since the Contractor was attempting to address an unforeseen site condition that was not reflected in the Architect's design and may have avoided delays and additional costs.
Evaluate the revisions for compliance with the design intent, contract documents, and applicable regulations, and require corrective action if the modifications are not acceptable.
Reject the revisions outright and automatically require demolition of the modified work regardless of its impact on the project.
n: The architect should evaluate the contractor's revisions against the design intent, the contract documents and the codes, and order corrective work if they are not acceptable. The contractor should have asked for clarification first. Source: CIAP Document 102 (UGCC), Discrepancies and Changes in the Work.

q: A project architect issues a specification section for interior partitions stating the exact gypsum board brand, the precise screw spacing, the required joint compound manufacturer, and the step-by-step installation sequence. The contractor later requests to substitute an equivalent ASTM-certified product, arguing that the specification did not explicitly prohibit alternates. Under standard specification classifications, what type of specification did the architect actually issue?
n: Naming the exact brand, fastener spacing, compound manufacturer and installation steps is a closed (prescriptive) specification. It leaves no room for substitutes. Source: CSI Project Resource Manual / Specifying Practice Guide (methods of specifying).

q: The architect issues a specification for a structural floor coating requiring a minimum compressive strength of 45 MPa, resistance to specific chemical exposures, and a 10-year service life under continuous industrial use. No brand, product, or installation method is mentioned. During bidding, one contractor proposes a polyurethane system, another proposes epoxy, and a third proposes a hybrid polymer system, all claiming compliance with the stated performance outcomes. Under standard specification classifications, what type of specification did the architect issue?
n: Stating only required results (strength, chemical resistance, service life), with no brand or method, is a performance specification. Any system that meets the results is acceptable. Source: CSI Project Resource Manual (methods of specifying).

q: An architect prepares the concrete works section of the project manual. Instead of listing the full mix design, curing procedures, slump tolerances, and reinforcement placement rules, the architect simply states: "All concrete works shall conform to ASTM C94 for ready-mixed concrete, ACI 318 for structural requirements, and ACI 301 for specifications for structural concrete." No brand, mix proportions, or installation methods are written. During construction, the contractor submits a mix design that technically complies with ASTM C94 but differs from the architect's usual preferred proportions. Under standard specification classifications, what type of specification did the architect issue?
n: Requiring only conformance to published standards (ASTM C94, ACI 318, ACI 301) is a reference specification. A mix that complies with those standards satisfies it. Source: CSI Project Resource Manual (methods of specifying).

q: An architect prepares the specification for a hospital's negative-pressure isolation room. Because the existing facility uses a specific pressure-monitoring system, the architect writes: "Provide [brand] Model 8630 Room Pressure Monitor, no substitutions," to ensure compatibility with the hospital's existing network. The contractor argues that an equivalent brand with the same features and UL certification should be acceptable because the specification did not describe performance criteria. Under standard specification classifications, what type of specification did the architect issue?
n: Naming one manufacturer's model with "no substitutions" is a proprietary (closed) specification, justified here by compatibility with the existing system. Source: CSI Project Resource Manual (proprietary specifying).
